title: Nervous and Endocrine Systems

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the structure and function of the nervous system, including the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.
- Describe the major endocrine glands, their hormones, and their basic functions.
- Recognize common nervous and endocrine conditions relevant to office communication.
- Apply knowledge of these systems to support safe, accurate communication, documentation, and escalation in the medical office.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the nervous system like the body's telephone wires. They carry messages very fast, like a text that arrives in a second, so you can react quickly.

### Question 2

The brain and spinal cord are like the main office of a company. All the other wires (nerves) run out from that main office to the rest of the body.

### Question 3

A neuron is like a tiny messenger cell that carries electrical notes from one place to another. Every message your brain sends or receives travels through neurons.

### Question 4

Dendrites are like the branches of a tree catching raindrops. They catch messages coming in and pass them toward the trunk (the cell body).

### Question 5

The axon is like the outgoing road on a one-way street. Messages leave the cell body and travel down this long road to the next stop.

### Question 6

Myelin is like the plastic coating around an electrical wire. It keeps the signal inside and lets it travel much faster without leaking.

### Question 7

The synapse is like the small gap between two dominoes, but instead of touching, one cell tosses a chemical 'note' across the gap to the next.

### Question 8

Neurotransmitters are like tiny chemical notes passed from one cell to the next across a tiny gap. Each note tells the next cell what to do.

### Question 9

The cerebrum is like the thinking and planning room of the brain — the biggest room, where ideas, words, and decisions are made.

### Question 10

The cerebellum is like the balance coach. It makes sure your movements are smooth and you don't tip over when you walk or reach for something.

### Question 11

The brainstem is like the building's engine room that runs quietly in the background, keeping the lights on — your breathing and heartbeat — without you thinking about it.

### Question 12

The spinal cord is like a busy two-way highway connecting the brain (the main office) to every neighborhood in the body, and it can also run quick automatic responses called reflexes.

### Question 13

The sympathetic system is like the body's alarm bell. When it rings, your heart speeds up and your eyes open wide so you are ready to react fast.

### Question 14

The parasympathetic system is like the body's calm-down button. It helps you relax, slows your heartbeat, and gets your stomach working again after the excitement is over.

### Question 15

The meninges are like three soft layers of bubble wrap wrapped around the brain and spinal cord to keep them safe.

### Question 16

Cerebrospinal fluid is like a water cushion inside a helmet. It floats the brain and spinal cord so they do not get bumped against hard bone.

### Question 17

Cranial nerves are like special wires that come straight out of the brain to run the face and senses — seeing, smelling, hearing, and moving your face.

### Question 18

The autonomic system is like the autopilot of the body. It keeps your heart beating and your food digesting without you having to remember to do it.

### Question 19

Sensory neurons are like the 'incoming mail' workers — they bring news from your skin, eyes, and ears up to the brain's main office.

### Question 20

Motor neurons are like the 'outgoing mail' workers. The brain writes a note, and motor neurons carry it out to the muscles to make them move.

### Question 21

Endocrine glands are like sprinklers that spray chemical messages straight into the river (the blood), so the messages can float to every part of the body.

### Question 22

Hormones are like letters sent through the mail (the blood). Each letter only gets opened by the right address — the target cell with the matching mailbox.

### Question 23

The pituitary is like the conductor of an orchestra. It waves the baton and tells the other glands when and how much to play.

### Question 24

The thyroid is like the body's thermostat for energy. Its hormone decides whether your body's 'engine' runs fast or slow.

### Question 25

Parathyroid hormone is like a 'calcium lifeguard.' When calcium in the blood dips too low, it helps pull more calcium back into the blood to keep levels steady.

### Question 26

Epinephrine is like a quick energy shot your body releases when you are scared or excited, helping you react in a flash.

### Question 27

Cortisol is like the body's long-acting stress manager. It keeps energy available and helps the body cope during longer periods of stress.

### Question 28

The pancreas makes two opposite helpers: insulin to bring sugar down and glucagon to bring sugar up, keeping your blood sugar just right.

### Question 29

Insulin is like a key that opens the doors of your cells so sugar can go inside and be used for energy, which lowers the sugar left in your blood.

### Question 30

Glucagon is like the emergency snack delivery. When blood sugar drops, it tells the liver to release stored sugar back into the blood.

### Question 31

The ovaries make two chemical messengers, estrogen and progesterone, that guide female development and the monthly cycle.

### Question 32

The testes are like the factory that makes testosterone, the chemical messenger that guides male development.

### Question 33

Melatonin is like the body's 'time to sleep' note. It goes up when it gets dark, helping you feel sleepy.

### Question 34

The thymus is like a training school where special immune cells (T-cells) learn to defend the body.

### Question 35

The hypothalamus is like a bridge and a boss. It takes messages from the brain and tells the pituitary gland what to release next.

### Question 36

Negative feedback is like a home thermostat. When the room gets warm enough, the heater clicks off so it does not get too hot.

### Question 37

A hormone is like a key that only fits certain locks. Even though the key floats everywhere in the blood, it can only open the cells that have the right lock.

### Question 38

ADH is like a water-saving switch. It tells the kidneys to hold onto water instead of flushing it all out as urine.

### Question 39

Growth hormone is like the body's 'grow bigger' message. It tells bones and muscles to grow, especially during childhood.

### Question 40

TSH is like a boss calling the thyroid factory and saying, 'Make more thyroid hormone, please!'

### Question 41

A stroke is like a roadblock cutting off delivery trucks to part of the brain. When brain cells don't get their supplies, they can get damaged quickly.

### Question 42

The 'T' reminds everyone that when it comes to a possible stroke, time is super important — like calling the fire department right away when you see smoke.

### Question 43

A TIA is like a car engine that stalls for a moment and then starts again. The problem went away, but it is a big warning that the engine needs attention.

### Question 44

A migraine is like a really strong storm in the head that can also make you feel sick to your stomach and bothered by bright lights and loud sounds.

### Question 45

Epilepsy is like a sudden electrical storm in the brain that can make a person's body move or act strangely for a short time, and it can happen more than once.

### Question 46

During a seizure, the safest thing is like being a careful helper: move sharp things away, watch the clock, and call a grown-up (the clinician) for help — never hold the person down.

### Question 47

In MS, the body's own defenders mistakenly strip the insulation off the brain's wires, so messages get slow or mixed up.

### Question 48

In Parkinson's, the brain slowly loses the cells that make a 'smooth movement' chemical called dopamine, so movements become shaky and slower.

### Question 49

Think of Parkinson's medicine like keeping a car's gas tank topped up. If you wait too long between fill-ups, the car sputters and stops working smoothly.

### Question 50

Alzheimer's is like a library where the books slowly become harder to find. Over time, it gets harder for the person to remember people and how to do everyday tasks.

### Question 51

Talking to someone with confusion is like guiding a lost friend gently — use simple words, go slowly, and let their helper stand beside them.

### Question 52

Bell's palsy is like one half of the face taking a sudden 'nap' — the muscles on that side become weak or droopy, but it often gets better over time.

### Question 53

Sciatica is like a pain signal running down a long nerve wire from your lower back all the way down your leg.

### Question 54

Peripheral neuropathy is like the long nerve wires to the feet getting fuzzy, so the feet feel numb or tingly instead of sending clear signals.

### Question 55

After a bump to the head, the brain is like a shaken snow globe. It needs a careful check by a professional before anyone says it is okay.

### Question 56

Meningitis is like a fire near the brain's protective wrapping. Fever, a bad headache, and a stiff neck are warning signs that need help right away.

### Question 57

Shingles is like the chickenpox germ 'waking up' later in life and causing a painful rash along the path of one nerve, usually on just one side.

### Question 58

Carpal tunnel is like a wrist 'traffic jam' squeezing the nerve that serves the thumb and first fingers, making them feel tingly or numb.

### Question 59

An EEG is like a microphone listening to the brain's electrical 'chatter' to see if there are unusual bursts that cause seizures.

### Question 60

A lumbar puncture is like taking a tiny sample of the watery cushion around the spinal cord to check if anything is wrong inside.

### Question 61

CT and MRI are like super-powered cameras that take pictures inside the head so doctors can see the brain without opening the skull.

### Question 62

Diabetes is like having too much sugar stuck in the blood because the 'key' (insulin) that lets sugar into cells is missing or not working well.

### Question 63

Type 1 is like the body's immune army accidentally knocking out its own insulin factory, while type 2 is like the body's doors ignoring the insulin key.

### Question 64

Low blood sugar is like a phone running out of battery — the person gets shaky, sweaty, and confused because the body is low on its main fuel.

### Question 65

If a person with diabetes suddenly looks pale, sweaty, and confused, it is like a car about to stall — you call for help right away and stay with them.

### Question 66

High blood sugar is like the body trying to flush out extra sugar through the kidneys, which makes a person very thirsty and need to urinate a lot.

### Question 67

An underactive thyroid is like a body heater turned down low — everything runs slower, so the person feels tired, cold, and gains weight.

### Question 68

An overactive thyroid is like a body engine revved too high — everything speeds up, so the person loses weight, feels hot, and their heart races.

### Question 69

A goiter is like the thyroid gland puffing up bigger than normal, sometimes making a visible swelling in the front of the neck.

### Question 70

Cushing's is like the body being stuck with its stress-hormone 'pedal' pressed down for too long, causing a range of changes from too much cortisol.

### Question 71

Addison's is like the adrenal factory running out of its important stress and salt-balance chemicals, leaving the body under-powered.

### Question 72

Acromegaly is like the body's 'grow' signal getting stuck on in an adult, so the hands, feet, and face slowly get bigger.

### Question 73

Think of thyroid medicine like a daily top-up that keeps the body's engine running evenly. The right way is always to follow the doctor's plan and ask them questions.

### Question 74

A1c is like a report card of your average blood sugar over the last few months, not just one day's score.

### Question 75

A fasting blood sugar test is like checking the gas gauge before you start the car in the morning — nothing added, so you see the true starting level.

### Question 76

Hashimoto's is like the immune system mistaking the thyroid for an intruder and slowly wearing it out, so it makes less thyroid hormone.

### Question 77

Graves' disease is like the immune system pushing the thyroid's 'on' button too hard, making it pump out too much hormone.

### Question 78

The word 'diabetes' just means lots of urination. In diabetes insipidus the problem is a water-balance hormone, while in diabetes mellitus the problem is blood sugar.

### Question 79

Calcitonin is like the 'calcium-down' helper, while its partner parathyroid hormone is the 'calcium-up' helper — together they keep calcium steady.

### Question 80

A pheochromocytoma is like an alarm-hormone factory stuck in the 'on' position, flooding the body with fight-or-flight chemicals that spike blood pressure.

### Question 81

Oxytocin is like the 'bonding and delivery' hormone — it helps the uterus squeeze during birth and helps milk flow when a baby feeds.

### Question 82

Cortisol is like the body's morning alarm — it naturally rises as you wake up to help you start the day, then fades at night so you can rest.

### Question 83

With diabetes, feet can lose their feeling, like a smoke alarm with weak batteries. Regular checks catch small problems before they become big ones.

### Question 84

If someone's speech slurs and their face goes numb on one side, it is like the brain sending an urgent SOS — you act fast and get emergency help.

### Question 85

Writing down symptoms is like taking a careful note for the doctor: use the patient's own words and add helpful details like when it happens and how it feels.
